title: Distinct Subsequences
description:
# Distinct Subsequences

Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` that are exactly equal to `t`.

A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more characters without changing the relative order of the remaining characters. Two subsequences are considered different when they use different indices from `s`, even if the chosen letters look the same.

The test cases are generated so that the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

Character matching is case-sensitive. A subsequence preserves order but may skip characters.

## Example 1:

**Input:** s = "rabbbit", t = "rabbit"
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** The three choices delete exactly one of the three consecutive `b` characters in `s`, producing `rabbit` each time.

## Example 2:

**Input:** s = "babgbag", t = "bag"
**Output:** 5
**Explanation:** There are five index sequences in `s` whose letters, in order, spell `bag`.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= s.length, t.length <= 1000`
*   `s` and `t` consist of English letters.
*   The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

solutions.name: Prefix Table Dynamic Programming
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a prefix table where `dp[i][j]` counts how many ways `s[0..i)` can form `t[0..j)`. For each source character, first inherit the count that skips it. If the character also matches the next target character, add the count that takes it.

## Key Insight

The recurrence separates the two legal decisions for every source index: skip this character, or use it as the next target character. Repeated letters are counted correctly because the table counts index choices rather than distinct text values.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: One-Row Reverse Target DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compress the prefix table into one array over target prefixes. `dp[j]` stores the number of ways to form the first `j` target characters after scanning the processed part of `s`. For each source character, scan `j` backward so the same source character cannot feed more than one target position in the same round.

## Key Insight

The two-dimensional recurrence only depends on the previous source row. Backward iteration preserves that previous-row value in `dp[j - 1]`, which is why repeated characters such as the three `b` letters are counted without double-using a single index.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Top-Down Take-or-Skip Memoization
solutions.description:
## Approach

Define `count(i, j)` as the number of ways to form `t[j..]` using only `s[i..]`. Every state can skip `s[i]`. If `s[i]` equals `t[j]`, the state can also take that character and advance both indices. Memoize the pair `(i, j)`.

## Key Insight

This is the most direct reading of the problem statement: each source index creates a binary choice, but many suffix states repeat. Memoization turns the exponential choice tree into one solved state per source-target suffix pair.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: Backward Suffix DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Fill a suffix table from the end of both strings. `suffix[i][j]` counts how many ways `s[i..]` can form `t[j..]`. The state always inherits the skip count from `suffix[i + 1][j]`, and matching characters add `suffix[i + 1][j + 1]`.

## Key Insight

The suffix view is the same recurrence as prefix DP but aligned with the natural base case: once all of `t` has been formed, every remaining suffix of `s` contributes exactly one completed subsequence.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(m * n)

solutions.name: Sparse Target-Index DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Group target positions by character. While scanning `s`, only update the target positions whose character equals the current source character, and visit those positions in reverse order. Here `k` is the average number of matching target positions for a processed source character and `A` is the fixed alphabet bucket count.

## Key Insight

The one-row DP does unnecessary work when most target positions do not match the current source character. Sparse buckets keep the same reverse-update invariant but restrict updates to positions that can actually receive new subsequences.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(m * k), worst-case O(m * n)
- Space Complexity: O(n + A)

tests.description: Canonical repeated-b example counts three different source-index choices.
Second canonical example has five valid index sequences.
Identical single-character strings have one subsequence match.
Choosing one source index from three equal letters gives three matches.
Choosing two ordered indices from three equal letters gives three combinations.
The entire source string is the only full-length match.
Disjoint strings have no matching subsequence.
Four choose three repeated-character case produces four matches.
The target is longer than the source, so no subsequence can match.
Five choose two catches off-by-one errors in repeated letters.
Repeated subsequence pattern requires counting index choices across both copies.
Repeated a and n letters create several valid ordered index choices.
Sparse target letters appear at multiple late positions.
Multiple e choices before the single t produce two valid subsequences.
